overview: Valdemar II of Denmark was king of Denmark at the height of medieval Danish power, remembered for Baltic expansion and later legal consolidation. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1202 — Becomes king; 1219 — Campaign in Estonia; 1227 — Defeat at Bornhöved.
He died in 1241, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Overview

He died in 1241, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Valdemar II of Denmark was born c. 1170. His family background is usually placed in House of Estridsen, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.

Valdemar II of Denmark's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Valdemar II of Denmark, called the Victorious, is remembered for both the height and the collapse of Danish Baltic dominance, and his reputation carries the drama of that reversal. He extended Danish power across the southern Baltic and into Estonia — Danish tradition tied the origin of the flag, the Dannebrog, to his crusade there — and codified law in the Code of Jutland, marking him as both conqueror and lawgiver.

The same reign was scarred by a humiliating episode that the sources dwell on: his capture by a vassal, Count Henry of Schwerin, during a hunting trip, and the long, costly captivity that followed, which shattered much of his Baltic empire. This combination of triumph and captivity gives his memory an unusual shape — the victorious king brought low by treachery and ransom.

What the record supports is an energetic and ambitious ruler, effective as both warrior and legislator, whose personal misfortune became central to how his reign was remembered. The epithet "Victorious" sits, pointedly, beside the disaster of his captivity, and the tradition preserves both without fully reconciling them.

contentSections.title: As king of Denmark
paragraphs: Valdemar II expanded Danish authority across parts of the Baltic. His reign also saw crisis after his capture in 1223 and defeat at Bornhöved in 1227, after which Danish dominance was reduced.
As King of Denmark, Valdemar II of Denmark had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died at Vordingborg in 1241; his death followed the issuing of the Law of Jutland and left a contested royal inheritance.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Valdemar II became one of Denmark’s most famous medieval kings, remembered for both expansion and the limits of imperial ambition.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Valdemar II of Denmark's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.
